Can countries expand power systems without deepening energy poverty?

Global electricity demand is projected to grow by around 3.6% annually through 2030, driven by electrification of industry, cooling, transport, and digital services. As countries expand grids and generation capacity to meet rising demand, the scale of investment required is substantial.

Yet this expansion coincides with a persistent access and affordability gap. While around 92% of the global population had basic electricity access in 2023, 666 million people still remained without electricity, with the access gap heavily concentrated in Sub-Saharan Africa.

But this moment is not only a development challenge — it is a strategic opportunity.
The acceleration of electricity demand can unlock new models of partnership, mobilize private capital at scale, and align infrastructure expansion with inclusive growth. With the right policy signals, regulatory clarity, and risk-mitigation instruments, private sector engagement can help close the financing gap while advancing affordability and equity.
Three approaches highlighted in UNDP’s From Commitments to Megawatts bulletin stand out:

💰 Implement targeted subsidies and financial mechanisms
Affordability remains a major barrier. UNDP analysis shows that only 22% of households without electricity can afford basic solar kits without support. Targeted subsidies can significantly expand uptake. In Togo, reducing PAYGo solar costs by 18–42% led to a 122% increase in adoption, with the strongest gains in underserved communities.

🔌 Scale decentralized renewable energy
Off-grid solar and mini-grids remain among the most cost-effective pathways to reach remote populations. These solutions have already provided electricity to over 560 million people globally, with the potential to reach nearly 400 million more by 2030 at lower cost than grid extension.

📊 Leverage data-driven energy planning
Data-driven tools such as least-cost power development planning enable governments to expand grids while prioritizing areas with the largest affordability and reliability gaps—ensuring that investments strengthen both capacity and inclusion.

UNDP is working with countries to translate these approaches into practical strategies—supporting integrated energy planning, financial de-risking, tariff reform, and decentralized renewable deployment that aligns infrastructure expansion with inclusive and sustainable development.

As electricity demand accelerates, the question is not only how fast systems grow—but whether expansion ensures affordability and equity.
